entities.name: Fulgentius of Ruspe
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Fabius Claudius Gordianus Fulgentius, better known as Fulgentius of Ruspe, emerged as a pivotal figure in North African Latin Christianity during the tumultuous 5th and 6th centuries CE. Born into a senatorial family in Telepte (modern Feriana, Tunisia) around 462 CE, his intellectual and spiritual formation occurred amidst the Vandal Kingdom's Arian rule, which profoundly shaped his theological focus. As Bishop of Ruspe, a see located in what is now Tunisia, Fulgentius became a staunch defender of Nicene orthodoxy and a leading exponent of Augustinian theology, particularly its doctrines on grace, free will, and predestination, against the persistent challenges of Arianism and semi-Pelagianism.

Fulgentius's episcopate was marked by repeated exiles under the Arian Vandal kings Thrasamund and Hilderic. His first banishment to Sardinia around 507 CE, alongside 60 other Catholic bishops, proved a period of intense literary output. From exile, he penned numerous treatises, dialogues, and letters, engaging directly with Arian theologians and systematically articulating Augustinian positions. Key works like *De veritate praedestinationis et gratiae* (On the Truth of Predestination and Grace) and *Ad Trasimundum regem libri tres* (Three Books to King Thrasamund) robustly countered Arian Christology, affirming the consubstantiality of the Son and his full divinity. His rigorous defense of Augustinian thought helped solidify its foundational status in Western theology.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Fulgentius of Ruspe played a crucial role in preserving and systematically articulating Augustinian theology against Arianism and semi-Pelagianism, thereby ensuring its continuity and influence within Latin Christianity during a period of significant political and theological upheaval in North Africa.
